subtype: Approach: writing a short letter when speaking feels hard [Action]
passage: Shreya, come and sit. Your mother says you have gone quiet about something. I know that quiet. I am Indu, and when I was a shy girl of eleven I wanted lessons at the town pool, but the words would not come out at the table. So I wrote a note in my best handwriting: "Dear Amma and Appa, I would like to learn swimming. The class is on Tuesday and Friday evenings, there is a lifeguard, and I will finish my homework first. Please think about it." I left it under the salt pot. They read it that night and said nothing, and I lay awake. Next morning Amma only said, "Let us go and see the pool together."

qa.q: Where did Indu leave the note for the parents?
qa.a: Indu left it under the salt pot.

qa.q: How did Indu feel that night after leaving the note?
qa.a: Anxious and hopeful, since Indu lay awake after the parents read it and said nothing.

qa.q: What other approach might work for a shy child, and why?
qa.a: A shy child could ask a relative to mention it first, because it lets a person get started without a face-to-face moment.

qa.q: How might Indu's parents have felt reading the note?
qa.a: Probably touched and thoughtful, since they said nothing that night but next morning suggested visiting the pool together.

grounding: Indu writes a polite note about swimming lessons and leaves it for the parents to think over.

subtype: Approach: writing a short letter when speaking feels hard [Action]
passage: The week Hansa wanted to ask, her parents were busy with Binita-masi's wedding, and the house was full of relatives and noise. Every time Hansa opened her mouth at dinner, someone else started talking, and she lost her nerve anyway. So on Tuesday night she tore a page from her notebook and wrote slowly: "Dear Mummy and Papa, the school is starting a swimming class on Saturday mornings. I want to join because I can't swim and I feel scared near water. There is a coach and a lifeguard. I will not miss any tuition. You don't have to answer now." She folded it and slipped it under Papa's spectacles case. Two days later, in the middle of the wedding chaos, Mummy squeezed her hand and whispered, "We read it. Yes."

qa.q: Why did Hansa choose to write a note?
qa.a: She felt shy and kept losing her nerve in the noisy house, so writing felt safer.

qa.q: What else could Hansa have done to be heard?
qa.a: She could have asked Binita-masi or another relative to help her find a quiet moment with her parents.

qa.q: How might Hansa's parents experience the note?
qa.a: They had time to read it and think without pressure, even in the wedding chaos, before saying yes.

grounding: In a busy, noisy week, a shy girl writes her parents a polite note about joining swimming, giving them time to decide.

subtype: Approach: writing a short letter when speaking feels hard [Action]
passage: Dilnaz practised the question in the mirror three times, and each time her throat closed up. Her parents weren't strict, but whenever she had to ask for something, her face burned. So after homework, in their Pune flat, she wrote on a sheet of blue paper: "Ammi and Abbu, my friend Leela's building has a swimming class on Sundays, 8 to 9. I'd like to join because I love water and want to swim properly, not just splash. It's near, and Leela's mother can walk us. Please think about it. You can tell me whenever you're ready." She stuck it on the fridge with the mango magnet and went to bed early. In the morning there was a second note under hers in Abbu's handwriting: "Thank you for telling us so clearly. Let's see the pool on Sunday."

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz stick the note?
qa.a: On the fridge, with the mango magnet.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when trying to ask aloud?
qa.a: Shy and nervous; her throat closed up and her face burned.

qa.q: What else could Dilnaz try if a note didn't work?
qa.a: Ask Leela's mother to mention the class to her parents, so the idea reaches them from an adult too.
With a calm note of his own, thanking her and suggesting they see the pool on Sunday. 🙂

grounding: A shy girl writes a polite note about joining a swimming class and leaves it for her parents to consider without pressure.
